title: Months 7 to 9: The Third Trimester
learningGoals: Know that your baby gains weight quickly and the brain and lungs mature in the last months
Know what early term, full term, late term and postterm mean, and why the last weeks matter
Know that most babies turn head-down before birth, and your care team checks position
Call your care team right away if your baby is moving less than usual

review.notes: Draft 2026-10-24 for the new How Your Baby Grows module, built around the March of Dimes month-by-month videos. Needs clinical review and every source confirmed against its slides. Sizes are rounded averages from ACOG's Changes During Pregnancy infographic. The movement slide reuses the reviewed wording from When to Contact Your Care Team. Head-down "by about 36 weeks" and the ACOG infographic's "major development finished by about 31 weeks" need the reviewer's check. Pictures are the reviewer's fetal and maternal development illustrations from the Pregnancy AI Assistant, padded to the class's 16:10 frame; that draft labeled the earliest stages in weeks after conception, while this class counts from the last period, so the pictures are placed by what they show.

slides.heading: Months 7 to 9: The Third Trimester
onScreen: How Your Baby Grows
slides.narration: Welcome to the last lesson in How Your Baby Grows. This one covers the third trimester, months seven to nine. Your baby is now putting on weight and getting ready for life outside the womb. We'll talk about what's still developing, why the last few weeks matter, how your baby gets into position for birth, and why your baby's movements are worth paying attention to.

visual.description: Side view cross-section of a pregnant body in the third trimester, the uterus filling the belly and pressing up toward the stomach and lungs.

slides.heading: Gaining weight, getting ready
onScreen: Major development is mostly done by about 31 weeks
Now your baby gains weight quickly
Fat under the skin helps keep your baby warm after birth
The brain and lungs keep maturing
slides.narration: By about thirty-one weeks, most of your baby's major development is done. Now your baby gains weight quickly. A layer of fat builds up under the skin, which will help keep your baby warm after birth. Your baby opens and closes their eyes, and the brain keeps growing fast. The lungs are among the last organs to be ready. They keep maturing right up to the end of pregnancy.

visual.description: Illustration of a fetus at about twenty-eight weeks, rounder now, eyes open, holding a foot.

slides.heading: Why the last weeks matter
onScreen: Your baby's brain, lungs and liver keep developing until 39 weeks and beyond
slides.narration: You may hear your care team use a few words for when a baby is born. Early term means thirty-seven weeks through thirty-eight weeks and six days. Full term means thirty-nine weeks through forty weeks and six days. Late term is forty-one weeks, and postterm is forty-two weeks or later. Babies born at thirty-nine weeks or later tend to do better than babies born earlier, because the brain, lungs, and liver are still developing in those last weeks. So unless there's a medical reason, a planned birth is best at thirty-nine weeks or later.

slides.heading: Your body: months 7 to 9
onScreen: Your uterus reaches up under your ribs
Less room for your stomach: heartburn is common
Less room for your lungs: you may feel short of breath
Your posture shifts, and your back may ache
slides.narration: In the last months, your uterus grows up toward your ribs. That leaves less room for everything else. Your stomach gets crowded, so heartburn is common. Smaller meals, and not lying down right after eating, can help. Your lungs have less room too, so you may feel short of breath. Your center of balance shifts forward, which can make your back ache. Trouble breathing that's sudden or severe, or chest pain, is different. Get medical care right away.

slides.heading: Getting into position
onScreen: Most babies turn head-down before birth
Your care team checks your baby's position
If your baby is bottom or feet first, you'll talk about options
slides.narration: Most babies turn head-down in the last weeks of pregnancy, usually by about thirty-six weeks. That's the best position for a vaginal birth. Your care team will check your baby's position at your visits. If your baby is bottom first or feet first, called breech, your care team will talk with you about your options.

visual.description: Illustration of a full-term baby curled head-down in the uterus, ready for birth.

slides.heading: When your baby drops
onScreen: In the last weeks, your baby may settle lower into your pelvis
Breathing gets easier
More pressure low down, and more trips to pee
In a first pregnancy, this can happen weeks before labor
slides.narration: Near the end, your baby may settle lower into your pelvis. This is called lightening, or your baby dropping. You may find it easier to breathe, because there's more room under your ribs. But you'll likely feel more pressure low in your pelvis, and need to pee even more often. In a first pregnancy, this can happen a few weeks before labor. In later pregnancies, it may not happen until labor starts.

visual.description: Side view cross-section at full term: the baby is head-down low in the pelvis, with small silhouettes showing the belly before and after the baby drops.

slides.heading: Call right away: baby moving less
onScreen: Get to know your baby's normal pattern
If movement slows, changes, or stops, call
Babies should still move during labor
Don't wait to see if it improves
slides.narration: By the third trimester, you'll start to learn your baby's usual pattern of movement. Babies don't run out of room to move near the end of pregnancy, and they should keep moving even during labor. If your baby is moving less than usual, the pattern changes, or you can't feel movement, call your care team right away. Don't wait to see if it gets better, and don't try to reassure yourself at home first. Your team can check on your baby quickly.

slides.heading: Quick check-in
slides.narration: Let's pause for a quick check-in.

question.prompt: You're 36 weeks pregnant and your baby has been much quieter than usual today. What should you do?
options: Wait until tomorrow; babies run out of room at the end
Call your care team right away
Mention it at your next visit
question.explanation: Babies don't run out of room to move. If your baby is moving less than usual, call your care team right away. They can check on your baby quickly.

slides.heading: What we covered
onScreen: Your baby gains weight; the brain and lungs mature
Full term is 39 to 40 weeks
Most babies turn head-down
Baby moving less? Call right away
slides.narration: Let's recap. In the third trimester, your baby gains weight quickly while the brain and lungs finish maturing. Full term is thirty-nine weeks through forty weeks and six days, and those last weeks matter. Most babies turn head-down before birth, and your care team will check. And if your baby is ever moving less than usual, call your care team right away. Next, a few review questions. Congratulations on finishing How Your Baby Grows.

reviewQuiz.explanation: Full term is thirty-nine weeks through forty weeks and six days. Thirty-seven to thirty-eight weeks is early term.

reviewQuiz.prompt: Near the end of pregnancy, babies move less because they run out of room.
reviewQuiz.explanation: False. Babies should keep moving right up to and during labor. If your baby is moving less than usual, call your care team right away.
